title: How Restart Your Consistency
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses one of SCM's most common reader questions: how to restart consistency after becoming inconsistent. He rejects the assumption that restarting must be an elaborately planned, high-anxiety event, arguing instead that if a classroom management plan has already been taught, restarting requires little more than a short, honest acknowledgment followed by immediate action. The article explains that in an inconsistent classroom, talk has become cheap, so extensive re-explaining accomplishes little; what actually convinces students is direct experience of renewed follow-through. He provides a short sample script for taking responsibility and announcing the change, and warns that students may push back harder initially, which teachers should expect and be prepared to weather. The piece closes by emphasizing that restarting consistency is fundamentally about action and unwavering commitment, not about finding the perfect words, timing, or strategy.
points: Restarting consistency after a period of inconsistency does not require an elaborately planned event; a short, honest acknowledgment followed by immediate action is sufficient.
In an inconsistent classroom, talk has become cheap, so extensive re-explaining accomplishes little compared to students directly experiencing renewed follow-through.
A brief sample script is offered: taking responsibility, then stating clearly that the classroom management plan will now be followed as written.
Students may push back harder initially when consistency resumes, and teachers should expect and be prepared to weather this resistance.
Restarting consistency is fundamentally an act of unwavering commitment and action, not a matter of finding perfect words, timing, or strategy.
quotes: The assumption is that it must be a big production. After all, the result of inconsistency is big misbehavior.
As long as your classroom management plan has already been taught, then it doesn’t take much to start over again. You see, in inconsistent classrooms talk is cheap.

I’m unhappy with how things are going, and it’s my fault. I haven’t protected your right to learn and enjoy being in this classroom. But it stops now. From this moment on, I will follow our classroom management plan as it’s written.

If you’re committed, if you’ve made the decision that there is no going back and you will be consistent even if it costs your job (it won’t), they’ll know it. They’ll feel it like a dachshund sensing a coming storm.
To be consistent, you must leap out of the plane. It’s a full-on, no-going-back vow of loyalty. Becoming consistent after not being so isn’t about perfect timing or preparation.
